summary:
Corse stands under France's national framework. National law on identity documents, criminal procedure, anti-discrimination, marriage and criminal law applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, and no Corse-specific finding on transgender detainees, border checks or hate violence appears in the sources; the national mechanisms documented below apply on the island unchanged.

Detention is the setting where the risk is documented most concretely. Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex inscribed on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities. As of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most of them at Fleury-Mérogis. Each facility improvises within that rule, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates, and treatment varies between establishments.

A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 and met with shouts of "We don't want any women here" despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. The same reporting documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend article D248. Accounts collected in that feature describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under isolation arrangements.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners and covering all places of deprivation of liberty. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women. The opinion documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health and social-care blind spots, reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across the prisons inspected, and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face. It references law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation and prison transfers and the racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination referents appointed since 2018.

The mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016, did not produce marked improvement in custody conditions according to the national preventive mechanism, which states that its 2021 opinion was necessary precisely because the 2010 opinion had gone unheeded. Reform of identity recognition and reform of placement practice are therefore separate questions for a visitor to weigh.

Placement practice is not uniform between establishments. Facilities variously use special units or isolation, and the inspection authority's findings identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention rather than a single national procedure.

Discrimination against trans people in everyday movement, accommodation and services is recorded by France's own oversight bodies as persistent rather than legally prohibited. The Défenseur des droits draws on case files and association testimony, and the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey puts identity-related discrimination reported by trans people in France at 64%.

Scope of protection has widened on paper: the inspection authority's remit now covers intersex and non-binary detainees, and racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination referents have been appointed in places of deprivation of liberty since 2018. Whether that widening reaches practice is not evidenced in the sources.

Remedy so far recorded is modest in scale. A 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, alongside a parliamentary question, indicates that challenge runs through litigation and the legislature rather than through automatic protection at the point of placement.
localsOnly:
Placement in custody is governed by article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which mandates separate establishments for men and women; the sex on identity documents decides the facility, and a foreign legal gender recognition is not recognised for that purpose. Trans women held under this rule are typically housed in men's facilities.

Access to treatment in custody is inconsistent between establishments. The inspection authority records health and social-care blind spots, discrimination and stigmatisation, and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion trans detainees face.

Isolation is used as a placement method and is identified as a structural problem, together with suicide prevention, in the national preventive mechanism's findings. Its 2021 opinion covers all places of deprivation of liberty and rests on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

Complaint routes in use include the Défenseur des droits, which has issued a framework decision on trans rights with official guidance for service providers, and the inspection authority, which has examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

Partner recognition rests on the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013. Anti-discrimination protection in services is supported by the referents appointed in places of deprivation of liberty since 2018 and by the framework decision's guidance to providers.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Corse-specific data on trans detainees, prison placement, border checks or hate-crime incidents is sourced; the findings above are national and are recorded as applying to Corse through the uniform national framework. Whether any trans detainee has been held in Corse, and under what placement, is unresolved.

Whether article D248 has been amended following the calls for amendment reported in 2018 is not sourced. The current text and any judicial or administrative gloss on it should be verified against the Criminal Procedure Code.

The outcome of oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly concerning Louna's placement, and whether her placement changed, is not sourced.

Border-check friction rests on a single first-person account of 7 March 2017. Frequency, current practice and any formal complaint or guidance on questioning trans travellers at French entry points are not sourced, and no account specific to Corse's airports or ports is available.

Whether the 2,000-euro symbolic award is representative of remedies available for detention conditions, and the current caseload of the Défenseur des droits on trans rights, are not sourced.
